claim: Post-transcriptional regulation plays important roles to fine-tune gene expression in bacteria.
source: Post-transcriptional regulation plays important roles to fine-tune gene expression in bacteria.
evidence: This is a general statement about bacterial gene regulation supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Regulation of type I toxin-antitoxin (TA) systems is achieved through sophisticated mechanisms involving toxin mRNA folding.
source: In particular, regulation of type I toxin-antitoxin (TA) systems is achieved through sophisticated mechanisms involving toxin mRNA folding.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and established knowledge in the field of type I TA systems.

claim: A genetic approach was set up to decipher the molecular underpinnings behind the regulation of a type I TA in Helicobacter pylori.
source: Here, we set up a genetic approach to decipher the molecular underpinnings behind the regulation of a type I TA in Helicobacter pylori.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: Lethality induced by chromosomal inactivation of the antitoxin was used to select mutations that suppress toxicity.
source: We used the lethality induced by chromosomal inactivation of the antitoxin to select mutations that suppress toxicity.
evidence: This describes the selection strategy used in the study.

claim: Single point mutations are sufficient to allow cell survival when the antitoxin is inactivated.
source: We found that single point mutations are sufficient to allow cell survival.
evidence: This is a key finding from the genetic selection experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Mutations located in the 5' untranslated region of the toxin hamper its translation by stabilizing stem-loop structures that sequester the Shine-Dalgarno sequence.
source: Mutations located either in the 5' untranslated region or within the open reading frame of the toxin hamper its translation by stabilizing stem-loop structures that sequester the Shine-Dalgarno sequence.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data including polysome fractionation, in vitro translation assays, and RNase H protection assays.

claim: Mutations located within the open reading frame of the toxin hamper its translation by stabilizing stem-loop structures that sequester the Shine-Dalgarno sequence.
source: Mutations located either in the 5' untranslated region or within the open reading frame of the toxin hamper its translation by stabilizing stem-loop structures that sequester the Shine-Dalgarno sequence.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data including polysome fractionation, in vitro translation assays, and RNase H protection assays.

claim: Short hairpins that sequester the Shine-Dalgarno sequence correspond to metastable structures that are transiently formed during transcription to avoid premature toxin expression.
source: We propose that these short hairpins correspond to metastable structures that are transiently formed during transcription to avoid premature toxin expression.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings and supported by in vivo DMS footprinting and covariation analysis.

claim: Co-transcriptional inhibition of translation is an additional layer of TA regulation in bacteria.
source: This work uncovers the co-transcriptional inhibition of translation as an additional layer of TA regulation in bacteria.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings showing that metastable structures form during transcription to prevent premature translation.

claim: Regulation of translation initiation via SD-sequestration has been reported for bacteriophage genes.
source: Regulation of translation initiation via SD-sequestration is an old theme that initially started with the study of bacteriophage genes (de Smit and van Duin, 1990) and ribosomal proteins (for a review see Duval et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Regulation of translation initiation via SD-sequestration has been reported for ribosomal proteins.
source: Regulation of translation initiation via SD-sequestration is an old theme that initially started with the study of bacteriophage genes (de Smit and van Duin, 1990) and ribosomal proteins (for a review see Duval et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: SD-sequence sequestration impacts the expression of sigma factors.
source: More recently, its impact on other bacterial genes such as sigma factors (Mearls et al., 2018) and translational riboswitches (Rinaldi et al., 2016) has been reported.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: SD-sequence sequestration impacts the expression of translational riboswitches.
source: More recently, its impact on other bacterial genes such as sigma factors (Mearls et al., 2018) and translational riboswitches (Rinaldi et al., 2016) has been reported.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Antitoxins belonging to type I TA systems do not directly interact with the toxin protein but rather prevent its expression.
source: In contrast to the largest type II TA family, antitoxins belonging to type I TA systems do not directly interact with the toxin protein but rather prevent its expression (Harms et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Type I TA regulation occurs through the direct base-pairing of the RNA antitoxin with the toxin mRNA and leads to toxin translation inhibition and/or mRNA degradation.
source: This regulation occurs through the direct base-pairing of the RNA antitoxin with the toxin mRNA and leads to toxin translation inhibition and/or mRNA degradation (Brantl and Jahn, 2015; Durand et al., 2012; Wen and Fozo, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The action of the RNA antitoxin is often not sufficient to avoid toxin expression.
source: However, the action of the RNA antitoxin is often not sufficient to avoid toxin expression (Masachis and Darfeuille, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Due to the coupling between transcription and translation occurring in bacteria, translation of the nascent toxin mRNA can potentially occur before antitoxin action.
source: Indeed, due to the coupling between transcription and translation occurring in bacteria, translation of the nascent toxin mRNA can potentially occur before antitoxin action.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about bacterial gene expression.

claim: A tight control of toxin synthesis is usually achieved via the direct sequestration of its SD sequence within stable stem-loop structures.
source: Thus, a tight control of toxin synthesis is usually achieved via the direct sequestration of its SD sequence within stable stem-loop structures (Masachis and Darfeuille, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The existence of a non-translatable toxin primary transcript is a major hallmark of type I TA loci.
source: The existence of a non-translatable toxin primary transcript is a major hallmark of type I TA loci.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about type I TA systems.

claim: In the non-translatable toxin primary transcript, the RBS occlusion occurs through the base-pairing of the SD sequence with a partially or totally complementary sequence termed anti-SD (aSD).
source: In this transcript, the RBS occlusion occurs through the base-pairing of the SD sequence with a partially or totally complementary sequence termed anti-SD (aSD).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about type I TA systems.

claim: aSD sequences are often located a few nucleotides (up to 11) upstream or downstream of the SD sequence and trap it within a hairpin structure.
source: Such aSD sequences are often located a few nucleotides (up to 11) upstream or downstream of the SD sequence and trap it within a hairpin structure.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about type I TA systems.

claim: In some cases, RBS occlusion involves an aSD sequence encoded far downstream and is achieved via a long-distance interaction (LDI) between the 5' and 3' ends of the toxin mRNA.
source: However, in some cases, RBS occlusion involves an aSD sequence encoded far downstream and is achieved via a long-distance interaction (LDI) between the 5' and 3' ends of the toxin mRNA (Gultyaev et al., 1997; Han et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The strategy of toxin expression regulation via the formation of a LDI has been recently described for a type I TA family of the Epsilon proteobacteria.
source: This strategy of toxin expression regulation via the formation of a LDI has been recently described for a type I TA family of the Epsilon proteobacteria.
evidence: This refers to previous work by the authors.

claim: The aapA/IsoA family is present in several copies on the chromosome of Helicobacter pylori.
source: This family, named aapA/IsoA, is present in several copies on the chromosome of the major human gastric pathogen Helicobacter pylori.
evidence: This is based on previous characterization of the aapA/IsoA family.

claim: The aapA1 gene codes for a small toxic protein whose expression is repressed by a cis-overlapping antisense RNA, IsoA1.
source: We characterized the aapA1/IsoA1 TA system at the locus I and showed that the aapA1 gene codes for a small toxic protein whose expression is repressed by a cis-overlapping antisense RNA, IsoA1 (Arnion et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Transcription of the aapA1 toxic gene generates a highly stable primary transcript whose translation is post-transcriptionally impeded by a 5'−3' LDI.
source: We have shown that transcription of this toxic gene generates a highly stable primary transcript whose translation is post-transcriptionally impeded by a 5'−3' LDI (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work and reference to a figure.

claim: A 3'-end ribonucleolytic event, termed 'mRNA activation step', is necessary to remove the LDI, thus enabling toxin translation.
source: Consequently, a 3'-end ribonucleolytic event, that we termed 'mRNA activation step', is necessary to remove the LDI, thus enabling toxin translation (Arnion et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The peculiar mRNA folding of aapA1 is strongly conserved at various loci in other related bacterial species.
source: We also showed that this peculiar mRNA folding is strongly conserved at various loci in other related bacterial species, clearly suggesting that this particular mode of control would also be conserved.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work and inference about conservation.

claim: Metastable structures are formed during mRNA transcription to prevent ribosome binding and avoid translation in some cases.
source: Previous work has shown that in some cases, metastable structures are formed during mRNA transcription to prevent ribosome binding and avoid translation (Lai et al., 2013; Zhu and Meyer, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In the absence of antitoxin expression, chromosomal toxin expression is lethal.
source: We first show that, in the absence of antitoxin expression, chromosomal toxin expression is lethal.
evidence: This is a key finding from the transformation experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: FASTBAC-Seq allows the mapping of intragenic toxicity suppressors within a given TA locus.
source: This method, that we previously named FASTBAC-Seq for Functional AnalysiS of Toxin-antitoxin in BACteria by deep Sequencing, allows the mapping of intragenic toxicity suppressors within a given TA locus (Masachis and Darfeuille, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Applying FASTBAC-Seq to the aapA3/IsoA3 TA locus revealed that single point mutations are sufficient to counteract the lethality caused by the absence of antitoxin.
source: Applying FASTBAC-Seq to the aapA3/IsoA3 TA locus revealed that single point mutations are sufficient to counteract the lethality caused by the absence of antitoxin.
evidence: This is a key finding from the FASTBAC-Seq experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: One-third of suppressors mapped to non-coding regions of the toxin mRNA.
source: Unexpectedly, one-third of suppressors mapped to non-coding regions of the toxin mRNA.
evidence: This is a finding from the FASTBAC-Seq analysis.

claim: Some suppressors target well-known regulatory elements, such as the toxin promoter and the SD sequence.
source: Some of them target well-known regulatory elements, such as the toxin promoter and the SD sequence.
evidence: This is a finding from the FASTBAC-Seq analysis.

claim: One suppressor located in the SD sequence does not act at the sequence level but at the mRNA structural level.
source: Remarkably, we show that one of the suppressors located in the SD sequence does not act at the sequence level but at the mRNA structural level.
evidence: This is a key finding from the characterization of the A40T suppressor mutation.

claim: The A40T mutation inhibits translation of the active mRNA by stabilizing an RNA hairpin in which the SD sequence is masked by an upstream-encoded aSD sequence (aSD1).
source: Indeed, this mutation inhibits translation of the active mRNA by stabilizing an RNA hairpin in which the SD sequence is masked by an upstream-encoded aSD sequence (aSD1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data including polysome fractionation, in vitro translation assays, and RNase H protection assays.

claim: A synonymous mutation within the Open Reading Frame (ORF) acts similarly to A40T but on another hairpin in which the SD sequence is masked by a downstream-encoded aSD (aSD2).
source: A synonymous mutation within the Open Reading Frame (ORF) acts similarly but on another hairpin in which the SD sequence is masked by a downstream-encoded aSD (aSD2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data including polysome fractionation, in vitro translation assays, and RNase H protection assays.

claim: Suppressor mutations reveal two transient hairpin structures that sequentially form during transcription and which are then replaced by a more stable LDI upon transcription termination.
source: These suppressor mutations reveal two transient hairpin structures that sequentially form during transcription and which are then replaced by a more stable LDI upon transcription termination.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: In addition to the post-transcriptional control achieved via a stable LDI, metastable structures are also required to prevent premature toxin expression in a co-transcriptional manner.
source: Our results indicate that, in addition to the post-transcriptional control achieved via a stable LDI, metastable structures are also required to prevent premature toxin expression in a co-transcriptional manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: IsoA3 is an 80 nucleotide antisense RNA encoded on the opposite strand of the AapA3 ORF.
source: Like other TA systems of this family, the aapA3/IsoA3 locus codes for an antisense RNA, IsoA3 (80 nucleotides), encoded on the opposite strand of a small ORF, AapA3.
evidence: This is based on the characterization of the aapA3/IsoA3 locus described in the manuscript and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The AapA3 peptide is 30 amino acids long.
source: The AapA3 peptide (30 amino acids) shares 60% sequence identity with the AapA1 peptide, whose ectopic expression is toxic in H. pylori (Arnion et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on the sequence analysis of the AapA3 ORF.

claim: The AapA3 peptide shares 60% sequence identity with the AapA1 peptide.
source: The AapA3 peptide (30 amino acids) shares 60% sequence identity with the AapA1 peptide, whose ectopic expression is toxic in H. pylori (Arnion et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison.

claim: Ectopic expression of AapA1 is toxic in H. pylori.
source: The AapA3 peptide (30 amino acids) shares 60% sequence identity with the AapA1 peptide, whose ectopic expression is toxic in H. pylori (Arnion et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Inactivation of the antitoxin promoter by introducing two point mutations in its −10 box was performed while maintaining the amino acid sequence of the toxin.
source: For this purpose, we inactivated the antitoxin promoter by introducing two point mutations in its −10 box, while maintaining the amino acid sequence of the toxin (Figure 1B, pIsoA3* in all figures), as previously described for the IsoA1 promoter (Arnion et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: No transformants were obtained when the antitoxin promoter was inactivated unless a non-sense or frameshift mutation was introduced in the aapA3 ORF.
source: However, no transformants were obtained unless a non-sense or frameshift mutation was introduced in the aapA3 ORF.
evidence: This is a key finding from the transformation experiments.

claim: In the absence of IsoA3 synthesis, the AapA3 toxin expression from its chromosomal locus is constitutive and too toxic to obtain a viable strain.
source: This result indicated that, in the absence of IsoA3 synthesis, the AapA3 toxin expression from its chromosomal locus is constitutive and too toxic to obtain a viable strain.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the transformation experiments.

claim: Two aapA3 mRNA species were detected in absence of IsoA3 expression: a long transcript of 225 nt (aapA3-FL) and a shorter transcript lacking the last 35 nt (aapA3-Tr).
source: Two aapA3 mRNA species were detected in absence of IsoA3 expression (Figure 1C, lanes 9 to 12): a long transcript of 225 nt, which was denoted aapA3-FL (full-length) and a shorter transcript lacking the last 35 nt (aapA3-Tr).
evidence: This is based on Northern blot analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The aapA3-Tr transcript was not detected in presence of IsoA3 RNA.
source: This latter was not detected in presence of IsoA3 RNA (Figure 1C, lanes 1, 2, 5–8) and corresponds to the truncated mRNA species previously described for the aapA1/IsoA1 homolog (Arnion et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on Northern blot analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Only the truncated mRNA (aapA3-Tr) is efficiently translated in vitro.
source: Translation assays demonstrated that only the truncated mRNA is efficiently translated in vitro (Figure 1D, lane 3).
evidence: This is based on in vitro translation assays shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Translation of aapA3-FL was close to the translational background obtained in absence of exogenous mRNA.
source: Translation of aapA3-FL (Figure 1D, lane 2) or of aapA3-FL containing a non-sense mutation in the start codon (Figure 1D, lane 4) was close to the translational background obtained in absence of exogenous mRNA (Figure 1D, lane 1).
evidence: This is based on in vitro translation assays shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The absence of IsoA3 leads to the accumulation of aapA3-Tr without affecting the amount of aapA3-FL.
source: Importantly, Northern blot analysis revealed that the absence of IsoA3 leads to the accumulation of aapA3-Tr without affecting the amount of aapA3-FL (Figure 1C lanes 9–12), indicating that IsoA3 specifically targets aapA3-Tr in vivo.
evidence: This is based on Northern blot analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: IsoA3 specifically targets aapA3-Tr in vivo.
source: Importantly, Northern blot analysis revealed that the absence of IsoA3 leads to the accumulation of aapA3-Tr without affecting the amount of aapA3-FL (Figure 1C lanes 9–12), indicating that IsoA3 specifically targets aapA3-Tr in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Northern blot analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In vitro structure probing confirmed that IsoA3 only interacts with the aapA3-Tr mRNA.
source: In vitro structure probing of the two AapA3 mRNA species further confirmed that IsoA3 only interacts with the aapA3-Tr mRNA (Figure 2, compare lanes 4–7 with 10–13).
evidence: This is based on in vitro structure probing experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: Base-pairing between IsoA3 and aapA3-Tr creates an extended RNA heteroduplex of 80 base-pairs.
source: Base-pairing between both transcripts creates an extended RNA heteroduplex of 80 base-pairs (Figure 2, lane 4) that is translationally inert, as shown by in vitro translation assays (Figure 1D, lanes 6–8).
evidence: This is based on in vitro structure probing and translation assays shown in Figures 1D and 2.

claim: The RNA heteroduplex formed between IsoA3 and aapA3-Tr is translationally inert.
source: Base-pairing between both transcripts creates an extended RNA heteroduplex of 80 base-pairs (Figure 2, lane 4) that is translationally inert, as shown by in vitro translation assays (Figure 1D, lanes 6–8).
evidence: This is based on in vitro translation assays shown in Figure 1D.

claim: None of the IsoA RNAs produced from the five other aapA/IsoA chromosomal loci (I, II, IV, V and VI) can replace the absence of IsoA3 expression.
source: Remarkably, none of the IsoA RNAs produced from the five other aapA/IsoA chromosomal loci (I, II, IV, V and VI) can replace the absence of IsoA3 expression demonstrating that their regulation is strictly module-specific, as previously suggested by in vitro translation assays (Sharma et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The regulation of aapA/IsoA modules is strictly module-specific.
source: Remarkably, none of the IsoA RNAs produced from the five other aapA/IsoA chromosomal loci (I, II, IV, V and VI) can replace the absence of IsoA3 expression demonstrating that their regulation is strictly module-specific, as previously suggested by in vitro translation assays (Sharma et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: IsoA3 represses aapA3 constitutive expression at the translational level by forming a stable RNA heteroduplex.
source: Altogether, these results show that IsoA3 represses aapA3 constitutive expression at the translational level by forming a stable RNA heteroduplex.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Inactivation of IsoA3 promoter led to a strong reduction (1.83 log-fold) in the fraction of StrR cells compared to that obtained with the WT or double-mutant start/pIsoA3* constructs.
source: As expected, inactivation of IsoA3 promoter led to a strong reduction (1.83 log-fold) in the fraction of StrR cells compared to that obtained with the WT or double-mutant start/pIsoA3* constructs (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on transformation efficiency experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In the absence of IsoA3, the chromosomal expression of AapA3 is highly toxic.
source: These results confirmed that in the absence of IsoA3, the chromosomal expression of AapA3 is highly toxic.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the transformation efficiency experiments.

claim: The number of streptomycin-resistant colonies obtained with pIsoA3* was slightly higher than that obtained when no DNA was used.
source: Notably, the number of streptomycin-resistant colonies obtained with pIsoA3* was slightly higher than that obtained when no DNA was used (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on transformation efficiency experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The StrR cells obtained in absence of DNA were all phenotypic revertants having mutated the rpsLCj gene.
source: The sequencing analysis revealed that the StrR cells obtained in absence of DNA were all phenotypic revertants having mutated the rpsLCj gene (Masachis et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on sequencing analysis and supported by a citation.

claim: Sequencing of the TA locus of approximately hundred pIsoA3* transformants revealed that all of them contained point mutations in the AapA3 ORF.
source: In contrast, sequencing of the TA locus of approximately hundred pIsoA3* transformants revealed that all of them contained point mutations in the AapA3 ORF (Masachis et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on sequencing analysis and supported by a citation.

claim: The genetic approach selected mutations that suppress toxicity allowing the generation of recombinant strains lacking antitoxin expression.
source: Thus, our genetic approach selected mutations that suppress toxicity allowing the generation of recombinant strains lacking antitoxin expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the sequencing analysis.

claim: 97.7% of the pIsoA3* transformants contained mutations.
source: Consistent with the above-mentioned first transformation assay, deep-sequencing data analysis showed that 97.7% of the pIsoA3* transformants contained mutations (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on deep-sequencing data analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A strong mutation rate (51.2%) was also observed with the WT PCR product.
source: A strong mutation rate (51.2%) was also observed with the WT PCR product (Figure 3C), which results from an unanticipated technical artifact linked to PCR amplification (see Material and methods section).
evidence: This is based on deep-sequencing data analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: More than half of the pIsoA3* transformed clones (51.8% out of ~5.1 million) were mutated at a single nucleotide position.
source: Analysis of the number of mutations per read in the complete sequencing dataset (all replicates combined) showed that more than half of the pIsoA3* transformed clones (51.8% out of ~5.1 million) were mutated at a single nucleotide position (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on deep-sequencing data analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Single point mutations are sufficient to abolish AapA3 toxin activity and/or expression.
source: This result demonstrates that single point mutations are sufficient to abolish AapA3 toxin activity and/or expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the deep-sequencing data analysis.

claim: A low number of pIsoA3* transformants (2.3%) had a WT locus sequence.
source: A low number of pIsoA3* transformants (2.3%) had a WT locus sequence (Figure 3C, pIsoA3* zero mutation), which can be explained by the sequencing error rate (around 1.5%) and/or suppressor mutations lying in regions outside the TA locus (i.e. outside the amplicon).
evidence: This is based on deep-sequencing data analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Single-nucleotide mutations were mainly substitutions, which are favored by PCR biases.
source: Single-nucleotide mutations were mainly substitutions, which are favored by PCR biases.
evidence: This is based on deep-sequencing data analysis.

claim: Only 4% of single-nucleotide mutations were insertions and deletions (indels).
source: Only 4% were insertions and deletions (indels).
evidence: This is based on deep-sequencing data analysis.

claim: Hierarchical clustering analysis revealed that the location and frequency of single substitutions were highly similar in the three biological replicates.
source: Hierarchical clustering analysis revealed that the location and frequency of single substitutions were highly similar in the three biological replicates, indicating that the locus coverage was close to optimum (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Single-nucleotide indels were almost exclusively present in the AapA3 ORF, generating truncated or longer forms of the peptide.
source: Contrary to substitutions (which were found in both coding and non-coding regions), the single-nucleotide indels were almost exclusively present in the AapA3 ORF, generating truncated or longer forms of the peptide.
evidence: This is based on deep-sequencing data analysis.

claim: The highest mutation densities were observed in the AapA3 ORF (53%), and in well-known regulatory regions such as the −10 box of the toxin mRNA (66.7%) and the SD sequence (42.8%).
source: Expectedly, the highest mutation densities (defined as the number of mutated nucleotides divided by the total number of nucleotides in the region of interest) were observed in the AapA3 ORF (53%), and in well-known regulatory regions such as the −10 box of the toxin mRNA (66.7%, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and the SD sequence (42.8%) (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is based on deep-sequencing data analysis shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: For the aapA3 −10 box, out of the six positions (5'-TAGGAT-3'), suppressor mutations were mostly found in the first two and last nucleotides.
source: For the aapA3 −10 box, out of the six positions (5'-TAGGAT-3'), suppressor mutations were mostly found in the first two and last nucleotides (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on deep-sequencing data analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The minimal functional aapA3 −10 box motif is 5'-TANNNT-3'.
source: This result allowed us to determine the minimal functional aapA3 −10 box motif 5'-TANNNT-3', which is in perfect agreement with the previously determined consensus sequence (Sharma et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the deep-sequencing data analysis and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: 17 mutations were unveiled in the 5' and 3' untranslated regions (UTR).
source: Remarkably, 17 mutations were unveiled in the 5' and 3' untranslated regions (UTR; Figure 3D).
evidence: This is based on deep-sequencing data analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Several point mutations in the UTRs created mismatch pairing, probably destabilizing two terminal stem-loops located at both ends of the active mRNA (aapA3-Tr).
source: Several of these point mutations created mismatch pairing, probably destabilizing two terminal stem-loop located at both ends of the active mRNA (aapA3-Tr) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on deep-sequencing data analysis and structural predictions shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Among the seven positions of the SD sequence (5'-AAAGGAG-3'), substitutions at the two central guanine nucleotides (positions +42 and +43) were the most frequently mutated in absence of antitoxin.
source: Among the seven positions (5'-AAAGGAG-3'), substitutions at the two central guanine nucleotides (positions +42 and +43) were the most frequently mutated in absence of antitoxin (Figure 4A), and one can deduce the minimal SD sequence to be 5'-AGG-3' or 5'-GGA-3'.
evidence: This is based on deep-sequencing data analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The minimal SD sequence can be deduced to be 5'-AGG-3' or 5'-GGA-3'.
source: Among the seven positions (5'-AAAGGAG-3'), substitutions at the two central guanine nucleotides (positions +42 and +43) were the most frequently mutated in absence of antitoxin (Figure 4A), and one can deduce the minimal SD sequence to be 5'-AGG-3' or 5'-GGA-3'.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the deep-sequencing data analysis.

claim: The transition G > A was preferentially enriched at positions +42 and +43, although the G > C and G > T transversion mutations were also selected.
source: As expected from PCR biases (Beaudry and Joyce, 1992), although the transition G > A was preferentially enriched in both cases, the G > C and G > T transversion mutations were also selected.
evidence: This is based on deep-sequencing data analysis and supported by a citation about PCR biases.

claim: A less-frequent transversion mutation (A > T) was selected within the SD sequence at position +40 (A40T).
source: Strikingly, a less-frequent transversion mutation (A > T) was selected within the SD sequence at position +40 (A40T, Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on deep-sequencing data analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Another unique transversion upstream of the SD sequence was identified (A28C).
source: Moreover, another unique transversion upstream of the SD sequence was identified (A28C, Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on deep-sequencing data analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The toxin full-length mRNA (aapA3-FL) is mainly found in non-ribosomal fractions (only 3% present in polysomes).
source: Polysome fractionation of this strain confirmed that the toxin full-length mRNA (aapA3-FL) is mainly found in non-ribosomal fractions (only 3% present in polysomes, lanes 10 to 14 in Figure 4B; see Figure 4—figure supplement 1 for quantification), whereas the truncated isoform (aapA3-Tr) is associated with the monosome and disome fractions (73% present in these fractions; Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on polysome fractionation experiments shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The truncated isoform (aapA3-Tr) is associated with the monosome and disome fractions (73% present in these fractions).
source: Polysome fractionation of this strain confirmed that the toxin full-length mRNA (aapA3-FL) is mainly found in non-ribosomal fractions (only 3% present in polysomes, lanes 10 to 14 in Figure 4B; see Figure 4—figure supplement 1 for quantification), whereas the truncated isoform (aapA3-Tr) is associated with the monosome and disome fractions (73% present in these fractions; Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on polysome fractionation experiments shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The absence of the aapA3-Tr form in heavier polysomes is probably due to the short length of the ORF (90 nt), which cannot accommodate more than two ribosomes.
source: The absence of the aapA3-Tr form in heavier polysomes is probably due to the short length of the ORF (90 nt), which cannot accommodate more than two ribosomes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the polysome fractionation results and knowledge about ribosome spacing.

claim: The aapA3-FL is indeed a translationally inert isoform, whereas the aapA3-Tr is translationally active.
